## Overview

`Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1` is a production-grade PowerShell cmdlet that
audits every Group Policy Object in an Active Directory domain and emits a
structured JSON evidence bundle. It is the designated **GPO input stage** for
the UIAO Drift Engine and can be consumed directly by an Evidence Ledger writer
or a Modernization Scoring pipeline.

The script requires no third-party modules — only the `GroupPolicy` and
`ActiveDirectory` RSAT modules that ship with Windows Server and Windows 10/11
Pro. It runs under standard domain user credentials with read-only access to
Group Policy and Active Directory.

::: {.callout-note}
This tool is **read-only**. It generates reports and evidence output. It makes
no changes to GPOs, OUs, or any other AD object.
:::

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Notes |
|---|---|
| PowerShell 5.1 or 7+ | Tested on both. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is sufficient. |
| RSAT: Group Policy Management | `Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.GroupPolicy.Management.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0` |
| RSAT: Active Directory DS | `Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0` |
| Domain read access | Standard authenticated domain user. No elevated privileges required. |
| Execution policy | `RemoteSigned` or `Unrestricted` in scope. See below. |

### Set execution policy (if needed)

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
```

### Install RSAT modules (Windows 10/11 client)

```powershell
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.GroupPolicy.Management.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name Rsat.ActiveDirectory.DS-LDS.Tools~~~~0.0.1.0
```

---

## Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-StaleDays` | `[int]` | `365` | Days since last modification before a GPO is flagged as stale. Accepted range: 1–3650. |
| `-OutputPath` | `[string]` | *(stdout)* | File path for JSON output. Omit to write to the pipeline or terminal. |
| `-Verbose` | switch | off | Emits progress messages: domain context load, OU count, GPO count. |

---

## Usage examples

### Quickstart — output to terminal

```powershell
.\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1
```

Writes a JSON array to stdout. Useful for piping into `ConvertFrom-Json` or
redirecting to a file manually.

---

### Write to a JSON file

```powershell
.\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 -OutputPath C:\Audit\gpo-audit.json
```

Writes UTF-8 encoded JSON and prints a three-line summary to the host:

```
Audit complete. Results written to: C:\Audit\gpo-audit.json
GPOs evaluated  : 147
GPOs with findings  : 63
Clean GPOs      : 84
```

---

### Custom staleness threshold

```powershell
.\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 -StaleDays 180 -OutputPath C:\Audit\gpo-audit-180d.json
```

---

### Verbose progress output

```powershell
.\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 -Verbose -OutputPath C:\Audit\gpo-audit.json
```

---

### Filter results in-shell — show only GPOs with findings

```powershell
$audit = .\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 | ConvertFrom-Json
$audit | Where-Object { $_.Rules.Count -gt 0 } |
    Select-Object GpoName, @{ N='RuleCount'; E={ $_.Rules.Count } } |
    Sort-Object RuleCount -Descending |
    Format-Table -AutoSize
```

---

### Export a flat CSV of all rule hits

```powershell
$audit = .\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 | ConvertFrom-Json

$audit | ForEach-Object {
    $gpo = $_
    $gpo.Rules | ForEach-Object {
        [pscustomobject]@{
            GpoName     = $gpo.GpoName
            GpoId       = $gpo.GpoId
            RuleId      = $_.RuleId
            Description = $_.Description
        }
    }
} | Export-Csv -Path C:\Audit\gpo-findings.csv -NoTypeInformation
```

## Output format

The script emits a JSON array. Each element represents one GPO.

```json
[
  {
    "GpoName": "Default Domain Policy",
    "GpoId":   "31b2f340-016d-11d2-945f-00c04fb984f9",
    "Rules":   []
  },
  {
    "GpoName": "Legacy Screensaver Policy",
    "GpoId":   "a1b2c3d4-0000-0000-0000-000000000001",
    "Rules": [
      {
        "RuleId":      "OBSOLETE_STALE",
        "Description": "GPO has not been modified in 892 days (threshold: 365).",
        "AgeDays":     892
      },
      {
        "RuleId":      "OBSOLETE_UNLINKED",
        "Description": "GPO has no links to any OU, domain, or site."
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

GPOs with no findings appear in output with an empty `Rules` array. The full
population is always present, making the output suitable for direct ingestion
without a separate "clean GPO" query.

---

## Rule reference

### `OBSOLETE_UNLINKED`

The GPO is not linked to any OU, domain root, or site. An unlinked GPO is
never applied and has no effect on any object in the directory.

**Remediation:** Delete the GPO, or link it to the appropriate target if the
absence of a link was accidental.

---

### `OBSOLETE_LINKED_TO_DELETED_OU`

The GPO is linked to an OU that no longer exists in the directory. The link
target is reported as `Target` in the rule output.

This condition arises when an OU is deleted without first removing GPO links,
which is a common oversight during OU restructuring projects.

**Remediation:** Remove the orphaned link using the Group Policy Management
Console (GPMC) or `Remove-GPLink`.

**Additional field:** `Target` — canonical path of the missing OU
(e.g. `contoso.com/Decommissioned/OldSites`).

---

### `OBSOLETE_NO_ENABLED_SETTINGS`

Neither the Computer Configuration nor the User Configuration section contains
any policy settings. The GPO exists in AD but delivers no policy.

This commonly results from a GPO that was created as a placeholder and never
configured, or from a GPO whose settings were removed without deleting the
object itself.

**Remediation:** Delete the GPO, or configure the intended settings.

---

### `OBSOLETE_STALE`

The GPO has not been modified since the configured staleness threshold
(`-StaleDays`, default 365). The actual age in days is reported as `AgeDays`.

Staleness alone is not proof of obsolescence — some GPOs are intentionally
stable. Use this signal in combination with other rules (e.g. unlinked + stale,
or no settings + stale) to prioritise remediation.

**Remediation:** Review the GPO. If still required, update its documentation.
If obsolete, delete it.

**Additional field:** `AgeDays` — integer days since last modification.

---

### `OBSOLETE_DISABLED`

A configuration section (Computer, User, or both) is disabled **and** that
same section contains no policy settings. A disabled section with active
settings is a valid intentional pattern and is not flagged.

**Remediation:** If the disabled section is intentional and permanent, delete
the GPO and create a replacement scoped only to the active section. If the
disable was accidental, re-enable the section.

**Additional field:** `Status` — one of `AllSettingsDisabled`,
`ComputerSettingsDisabled`, `UserSettingsDisabled`.

---

### `OBSOLETE_ORPHAN_WMI_FILTER`

The GPO references a WMI filter by GUID, but no matching WMI filter object
exists in Active Directory. WMI filters are stored as AD objects under
`CN=SOM,CN=WMIPolicy,CN=System,<DomainDN>`.

When the referenced filter is missing, the GPO will not apply to any computer
regardless of link or scope — Windows treats a missing WMI filter as a failed
evaluation.

**Remediation:** Either recreate the WMI filter with the matching GUID, assign
a different existing filter, or remove the filter reference from the GPO.

**Additional fields:** `WmiFilter` — display name of the missing filter.
`FilterDN` — the expected Distinguished Name in AD.

---

### `EVIDENCE_ERROR`

The script could not generate or parse the GPO's XML report. This is an
instrumentation failure, not an obsolescence signal. The `Error` field contains
the exception message.

Common causes: insufficient SYSVOL access, a corrupted GPO template in SYSVOL,
or a GPO that exists in AD but whose SYSVOL folder has been manually deleted.

**Remediation:** Investigate the error. If the SYSVOL template is missing,
the GPO may need to be force-deleted and recreated.

**Additional field:** `Error` — exception message from `Get-GPOReport`.

## Integration with UIAO

The JSON output from this script maps directly to UIAO core architecture
components.

### Drift Engine input

Each rule hit is a **drift event**. The `RuleId` field is the drift signal
type. Feed the output to the Drift Engine as follows:

```powershell
$evidence = .\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 | ConvertFrom-Json

$driftEvents = $evidence | ForEach-Object {
    $gpo = $_
    $gpo.Rules | ForEach-Object {
        [pscustomobject]@{
            ObjectId    = $gpo.GpoId
            ObjectName  = $gpo.GpoName
            ObjectType  = 'GroupPolicyObject'
            DriftSignal = $_.RuleId
            Detail      = $_
            DetectedAt  = (Get-Date -Format 'o')
        }
    }
}
```

### Evidence Ledger

The full JSON array (including GPOs with no findings) is an OSCAL-aligned
evidence bundle. Each GPO is a `component` observation with `findings`
populated from the `Rules` array. GPOs with an empty `Rules` array satisfy
their corresponding control objectives with no findings.

### COR baseline population

`GpoId` is a stable, system-assigned GUID — suitable as the `CorId` for a
Group Policy Object record in the Canonical Object Record schema. Use
`OBSOLETE_*` rule hits to set `DriftStatus: DRIFTED` and `EVIDENCE_ERROR` hits
to set `DriftStatus: UNKNOWN`.

## Scheduling and automation

### Run as a scheduled task (daily audit)

```powershell
$action  = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'pwsh.exe' `
               -Argument '-NonInteractive -File C:\Scripts\Invoke-GpoObsoleteAudit.ps1 -OutputPath C:\Audit\gpo-audit.json -StaleDays 365'

$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At '02:00'

$principal = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId 'CONTOSO\svc-uiao-audit' `
                 -LogonType ServiceAccount -RunLevel Limited

Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'UIAO GPO Obsolete Audit' `
    -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Principal $principal
```

The service account requires only domain read permissions. No local admin or
Group Policy write rights are needed.

## Frequently asked questions

**Does the script modify any GPOs or AD objects?**
No. Every operation is read-only. No changes are made to any GPO, link, OU, or
WMI filter.

**How long does it take?**
Approximately 1–3 seconds per GPO depending on SYSVOL latency. A domain with
200 GPOs typically completes in 4–10 minutes.

**Can I run this against a remote domain?**
Yes, if your workstation is domain-joined or you pass credentials via
`Enter-PSSession` / `Invoke-Command` on a DC or member server in the target
domain.

**What permissions does the service account need?**
Read access to Group Policy objects (default for authenticated users) and read
access to Active Directory OUs and WMI filter objects (also default). No
additional delegation is required in standard environments.

**Why do some GPOs show `OBSOLETE_STALE` even though they look current in GPMC?**
The `ModificationTime` property reflects the last time a GPO's settings were
written, not the last time it was viewed or linked. A GPO linked to a new OU
but never re-saved retains its original modification timestamp.

**The script reports `EVIDENCE_ERROR` for a few GPOs. What does that mean?**
The GPO exists in Active Directory but its corresponding SYSVOL template folder
is missing or inaccessible. This is a pre-existing condition in the environment,
not a script issue. Investigate those GPOs directly in GPMC.
